Stress with Suffixes: Two Syllables Before the Suffix

Sometimes, stressed syllables based on suffixes appear to not follow any pattern at all.
But, when you look at words in reverse, from the end of the word toward the front, a pattern emerges.
These patterns can help you become familiar with how certain words are pronounced.
Stress patterns can only be found when it is understood that syllables must be counted from the end of the word toward the beginning of the word.

Let's look at the words accommodate, investigate and unfortunate. They all end in the suffix -ate. When you read them aloud, they do not necessarily follow a pattern.  But, try looking at them in reverse. You will notice a pattern.

The pattern with these kinds of words is that they are stressed on the second syllable back from the suffix.
Other suffixes which follow this rule are:

-ate
-acy
-ize
-tion
For example:

accommodate
investigate
realize
unfortunate
efficiency
recognize
Try reading these sentences from the text. Focus on saying the words with these suffixes correctly:
How can I accommodate you today?
Could you please investigate the text message capability?
I didn't even realize this was happening.
That's really unfortunate but I can troubleshoot that issue for you.
The efficiency of these tests is very good.
I ran the tests and they didn't recognize any corruption or infection with a virus.
Intonation with Either/ Or Questions

Intonation is an important feature of pronunciation. It is the rise and fall (the melody) of your voice. Depending on what you want to communicate, you need to choose the proper intonation.

Either/or questions aim to get the listener to choose one of two or more explicitly stated options rather than provide a simple yes or no.
Either/ or questions function as information questions (the listener needs to provide an informative answer, not just yes or no). For this reason, they end with a falling intonation.
For example:
Do you want soup ⤴ or salad ⤵?
Questions with more than two options follow the intonation pattern typical of lists.
For example:
Do you want soup ⤴ , salad ⤴ or bread ⤵?

Tech: Hi there. How can I accommodate you today? Do you need sales or service?
Peter: Service please. I'm having problems with my laptop and my cell phone. I was wondering if you could check my devices.
Tech: Sure. Is your phone Android or iOS?
Peter: It's iOS. Could you please investigate the text message capability? I can't send text messages properly. People receive them days after I send them. I didn't even realize this was happening.

Tech: That's really unfortunate but I can troubleshoot that issue for you.
Peter: Also, there's something strange going on with my laptop. I had a file saved on my desktop and then it just disappeared into thin air. Do you think it was a computer virus, or a corrupt file or something else?
Tech: I'll run a diagnostic test for a virus. I could also check to see if the hard drive is corrupt. The efficiency of these tests is very good. I'll take them to the back to run the tests. I'll be back in a few minutes. What is the name of the lost file?
Peter: Proposal December 2015.
Vanessa: Well, she seems confident that she can help. I don't think you need to worry.

Tech: So, I ran the tests and they didn't recognize any corruption or infection with a virus. I found no problems at all. In fact, I found your file. On the desktop.
Peter: What? That's impossible. I swear it wasn't there and I searched everywhere.
Tech: Well, it's there now. Try sending me a text to 555-567-0987.
Peter: Okay. There you go.
Tech: I got it. Your phone is fine. Do you want to pay for the service with cash, credit or debit?
Peter: I can't believe it.
Vanessa: So it's not your devices, it's you!
Peter: I know what it is. Mercury's in retrograde!
